mainText:
If you only remember one thing: A I is moving from chatbots to agents that do work for you, and regulators are arguing over who sets the rules.

Number one. A I products and money.

Google unveiled a single Gemini agent for work. You give it objectives, not just instructions. It connects to Workspace, Microsoft three sixty five, Slack, and Jira. Each agent gets its own account and email, and its actions are logged under its own name. It starts with businesses, and consumers come later. Why it matters: agents with their own identities raise new questions about accountability.

From your Rundown: a startup called Atomic Machines came out of stealth with two hundred fifty million dollars. It builds tiny machines straight from code. Think vibe coding, but for hardware. Its first product is a fingertip sized power switch for A I data centers. Why it matters: it could change how hardware gets made.

Also from the Rundown: Microsoft's chief executive says to treat A I as if it has already been hacked.

Number two. A I policy.

Microsoft president Brad Smith says everyday products, like dairy, get more oversight than A I. He wants mandatory breach alerts, outside evaluators, and kill switches. He says the U K is best placed to lead. The U K's A I Security Institute says it can still test the newest models, despite reports that the White House asked labs to hold them back. Why it matters: voluntary pledges versus binding rules is the central fight.

Number three. China and chips.

From your China A I Weekly Digest. DeepSeek is raising at least twelve billion dollars, backed by Tencent, and possibly up to fifteen billion. Manus raised over five hundred million after splitting from Meta. Kling is reportedly picking banks for an I P O of more than one billion dollars. The U S issued its first outbound investment fine over a Chinese robotics A I deal. And hackers reportedly used a Chinese A I agent tool to breach South Korean banks. Why it matters: Chinese A I is raising frontier scale money while the U S tightens investment rules.

Number four. Tech for good.

The International Rescue Committee, writing in Fortune, describes A I pilots that help teachers over WhatsApp, use satellite images to find children missed by the census, and improve malnutrition data. In testing, one assistant's pass rate rose from fifty two to seventy seven percent. It still fails about one answer in four, so humans review every response. Why it matters: it's a model for responsible A I in high stakes settings.

Number five. Also in your reads. The New Yorker asks, should cars just drive themselves? It looks under the hood at Waymo.

The thread today: agents are getting more power, and everyone is asking for human oversight. Have a great day.
